overview: Arapaho history includes distinct northern and southern communities, skilled making, family relationships and a living language. Homes, museum objects and recorded voices help us explore particular lives across generations.

periods.title: Earlier histories and Plains communities
periods.summary: Arapaho histories recall movement from the northeast, with uncertain early routes and dates. Eighteenth-century reports describe related communities. The map’s 1492 opening is not a founding date.

periods.title: Trade, treaties and increasing pressure
periods.summary: Northern and southern groups developed around different trading connections. The 1851 Fort Laramie treaty defined a territorial framework; the Colorado gold rush after 1858 intensified settler pressure and conflict.

periods.title: Massacre and displacement
periods.summary: On November 29, 1864, Colorado troops attacked Cheyenne and Arapaho civilians at Sand Creek. Southern Arapaho communities subsequently moved to Indian Territory, now Oklahoma. Northern Arapaho arrived at Wind River in 1878.

periods.title: Reservation life and coercive schooling
periods.summary: At Wind River, reservation policies brought land loss. Boarding and mission schools pressured children to abandon their language and customs.

periods.title: Community renewal and language teaching
periods.summary: Cultural renewal strengthened from the 1960s and 1970s. Continuing efforts include community-directed education and language teaching for both children and adults.

sections.title: Objects made for care, work and art

items.text: A Northern Arapaho cradleboard in the Smithsonian collections is dated to about 1890. It combines wood, hide, cotton canvas, sinew and porcupine-quill decoration. The catalogue records collection from Elizabeth Sunroad at Wind River in 1924. It preserves skilled sewing and quill work in a baby carrier, but the record does not name its maker or the child it carried.

A hide scraper from Wind River joins an antler body to an iron blade. The museum places it in a group collected from five Northern Arapaho people in 1923. This practical tool combines materials with different origins. Its history of collection does not establish its manufacture date or which of those five people owned this individual scraper.

Donna Shakespeare-Cummings made a doll dated to about 2000 that brings together hide, glass beads, porcupine quills, wood and other materials. Its construction includes sewing, carving, painting and beadwork. A small figure can hold a remarkable amount of skilled work. This museum artwork is evidence of a named Northern Arapaho artist’s practice, not proof that a child used it as a toy.

Agnes Yellow Plume and Ann Wolf recalled making toy horses from bent willow, with weed tails and little rawhide saddles. Dolls rode them on pretend journeys, sometimes with tiny tipi poles. Their memories, published in 1952, show children turning familiar travel into play. A twig could become transport for an entire imaginary household.

Ann Wolf remembered a lifelong friendship that began at boarding school. The two women exchanged clothing and other gifts; their husbands became friends too. Agnes Yellow Plume described a group of friends instead of one closest companion. Their accounts show variation within a community, not a rule that everyone must have exactly one best friend.

Hilger’s interviews also recorded ordinary baby care: some mothers recalled powdered, aged buffalo dung as absorbent cradle filling and sitting toddlers on a can during toilet training. These are historical accounts from particular women, not evidence that the practices were universal, safe or medically effective.

sections.title: Homes, food and the surrounding land

items.text: In Boulder’s ethnographic report, Arapaho representatives explain why camps could not all remain together: people and horses needed water and food. Smaller family camps and larger gatherings served different purposes. Frank Medicine Water describes journeys between water sources. Planning where to sleep also meant planning where a horse could drink; the travel arrangements included thirsty passengers with four legs.

The Arapaho Language Project records food plants including chokecherries, serviceberries, wild onions and biscuitroot. Buffalo mattered greatly, but gathering required knowledge of a varied landscape too. This list identifies documented foods; it does not tell us what every family ate on a particular day.

In research published in 2023, Northern Arapaho elders explored places and a tipi through virtual reality. A 2019 session showed Nii’eihii Neecee’s view on a large screen so others could follow. Working with the Language and Culture Commission, researchers used these settings to prompt speech and memories. The virtual world supported learning from elders; it did not replace their knowledge.

The Cheyenne and Arapaho Tribes describe language classes in their communities and online, outreach to Head Start and child-care programmes, and intensive adult learning with experienced speakers. Language work crosses generations: children learn, adults practise and elders contribute knowledge. Sharing a tribal government does not make Cheyenne and Arapaho the same language.

In its January 2025 description, the Cheyenne and Arapaho Buffalo Program reports quarterly distributions of buffalo meat, recipes and food information to elders and eligible members, including people with diabetes or at risk of it. The programme also supports herd restoration. This describes community food provision, not a claim that one food cures a disease.

In 2000, manuscript copies of letters by Silas Soule and Joseph Cramer were found in Denver. The National Park Service explains that these eyewitness accounts document the Sand Creek Massacre and soldiers who resisted participating. Written evidence helps examine what happened alongside the continuing work of descendant communities to remember the people who were killed.

ending.text: Arapaho communities continue at Wind River in Wyoming and within the Cheyenne and Arapaho Tribes in Oklahoma. Displacement changed political life without ending the people. Families, institutions and language teaching continue; 1783 is only this map entry’s endpoint.
